claim: AC 150/5300-13B governs approach and departure surface design standards for civil airports, including Tables 3-2 through 3-5 defining surface dimensions and slopes for precision-instrument runways.
supporting_excerpt: Updated approach surface discussion in paragraph 3.6.1 and added new approach and departure surfaces Figure 3-5, Figure 3-6, and Figure 3-7. Updated departure surface to reflect forthcoming Terminal Instrument Procedures (TERPS) criteria in paragraph 3.6.2 and revised approach and departure surface values in Table 3-2, Table 3-3, Table 3-4, and Table 3-5.
caveat: Specific surface dimensions for RWY 19R/1L at IAD would require review of the current FAA-approved ALP and instrument approach/departure procedure criteria.

claim: FAA's September 2022 Policy Guidance on Approach and Departure Surface Protection establishes that surface protection obligations extend beyond physical height penetration — sponsors must protect these corridors from development that forecloses future runway extension, procedure modification, or threshold repositioning.
source_title: Policy Guidance: Approach and Departure Surface Protection
supporting_excerpt: ARP is to object if any obstacles penetrate the standard departure surface as described in AC 150/5300-13, Airport Design. To maintain land use compatibility around airports and protect surfaces associated with instrument and visual operations of the airport, it is recommended to protect terminal airspace by clearing bushes and trees that penetrate or have the potential to penetrate any applicable navigable surfaces.
caveat: The full text of the policy guidance PDF could not be fetched directly (403 Forbidden). The document exists and its index page was confirmed. Content citations are drawn from search-result extracts.

claim: FAA ARP SOP 2.00 requires ADO review of any ALP change against three safety criteria: (A) materially impacts safe and efficient aircraft operations; (B) adversely affects safety of people or property on ground from aircraft operations; (C) adversely affects the value of prior federal investments.
source_title: FAA Airports ARP SOP 2.00 — ALP Review
supporting_excerpt: FAA retains authority to review and approve only those ALP changes that (1) materially impact the safe and efficient operation of aircraft, (2) adversely affect the safety of people or property on the ground as a result of aircraft operations, or (3) adversely affect the value of prior Federal investments to a significant extent.
caveat: SOP 2.00 has been subject to updates related to FAA Reauthorization Act 2024 Section 743, which limits FAA non-aeronautical development review but explicitly retains FAA jurisdiction over federally acquired/conveyed land and safety-affecting development.

claim: 14 CFR §139.311 requires airport certificate holders to ensure all lighting on the airport — including for buildings, aprons, vehicle parking areas, roadways, and fuel storage areas — is adequately adjusted or shielded to prevent lighting interference.
supporting_excerpt: Each certificate holder must ensure that all lighting on the airport, including that for aprons, vehicle parking areas, roadways, fuel storage areas, and buildings, is adequately adjusted or shielded to prevent lighting interference.
caveat: Regulation applies to airport-owned/controlled lighting. Whether a proposed data center's lighting would be governed by this provision depends on lease terms and MWAA operational control over the site.

claim: FAA AIM §7-6-16 warns that cooling tower exhaust plumes can extend more than 1,000 feet above the structure and that encounters may include airframe damage, aircraft upset, and engine damage/failure, with effects most pronounced during low-altitude flight in calm and cold air near approach and departure corridors.
source_title: FAA Aeronautical Information Manual §7-6-16 — Avoid Flight in the Vicinity of Exhaust Plumes (Smoke Stacks and Cooling Towers)
supporting_excerpt: Results of encountering a plume may include airframe damage, aircraft upset, and/or engine damage/failure. These hazards are most critical during low altitude flight in calm and cold air, especially in and around approach and departure corridors or airport traffic areas. Studies predict that the significant turbulent effects of an exhaust plume can extend to heights of over 1,000 feet above the height of the top of the stack or cooling tower.
caveat: There are no FAA regulations establishing mandatory separation distances for thermal exhaust plumes; AIM guidance is advisory. The FAA's Technical Guidance Assessment Tool for Thermal Exhaust Plume Impact provides a more detailed engineering framework but was not confirmed to specifically cite data centers.

claim: AC 150/5200-33C prohibits new water impoundments of one-quarter acre or larger within an approach corridor and within 5,000 feet of the runway end, and recommends a 5-statute-mile buffer from the airport boundary for attractants that could draw wildlife into approach or departure airspace.
source_title: Advisory Circular 150/5200-33C — Hazardous Wildlife Attractants on or near Airports
page_or_section: Sections on stormwater detention and approach/departure airspace buffers
supporting_excerpt: No new water impoundments of one-quarter acre or larger shall be allowed within an approach corridor and within 5,000 feet from the end of the runway. The FAA recommends a distance of 5 statute miles between the farthest edge of the airport's AOA and the hazardous wildlife attractant if the attractant could cause hazardous wildlife movement into or across the approach or departure airspace.
units: Feet (5,000 from runway end); acres (1/4 acre impoundment threshold); statute miles (5-mile approach/departure buffer)
caveat: The 5,000-foot rule applies to retention within an approach corridor — both conditions must be met simultaneously. The specific distance of the proposed stormwater facility from the RWY 19R runway end has not been confirmed in available public documents.

claim: AIP Grant Assurances #19 (Operation and Maintenance), #20 (Hazard Removal and Mitigation), #21 (Compatible Land Uses), #22 (Economic Nondiscrimination), and #29 (Airport Layout Plan) are at risk from incompatible non-aeronautical development within approach/departure surfaces without FAA ADO concurrence.
source_title: FAA Order 5190.6C — Airport Compliance Manual, Chapter 20
supporting_excerpt: Grant Assurance 21 requires airports to take appropriate action, to the extent reasonable, including the adoption of zoning laws, to restrict the use of land adjacent to or in the immediate vicinity of the airport to activities and purposes compatible with normal airport operations, including landing and takeoff of aircraft. A sponsor found in violation faces corrective-action orders, potential withholding of future AIP grants, and possible grant-repayment requirements.
caveat: Specific grant assurance applicability to this parcel depends on whether it was acquired with federal AIP funds or conveyed from federal surplus property. MWAA's federal lease and enabling legislation impose additional obligations beyond standard AIP grant assurances.

claim: A Part 16 complaint by any aggrieved aeronautical user (including airlines certificated at IAD) can trigger FAA enforcement of grant assurance violations, with sanctions including corrective-action orders, withholding of future AIP grants, and grant repayment.
source_title: 14 CFR Part 16 — Rules of Practice for Federally Assisted Airport Proceedings
supporting_excerpt: An aggrieved party who has been adversely impacted by an airport that has maintained or operated airport facilities in violation of these grant assurances may bring an enforcement action against the airport under 14 C.F.R. 16. A sponsor found in violation faces corrective-action orders, potential withholding of future AIP grants, and possible grant-repayment requirements.
caveat: Most common Part 16 cases involve revenue diversion and exclusive-rights violations; incompatible land use cases are less frequent but are adjudicated under the same framework.

claim: MWAA's 2018 sale of 424 acres of Western Lands at IAD to Digital Realty for $236.5 million represents a correctly sited data center precedent — the Western Lands site is positioned outside IAD's approach and departure surfaces, in a corridor excluded from residential development by Loudoun County noise overlay.
source_title: Data Center Developer To Buy 424-Acre Site Next To Dulles Airport
source_type: Industry press (corroborated by MWAA press release)
supporting_excerpt: The Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority Board of Directors voted to approve the sale of 424 acres adjacent to Washington Dulles International Airport, known as the Western Lands, to Digital Realty for $236.5 million. The area is in a zone where by policy the county does not allow residential development due to airport noise, making it ideally suited for industrial data center operations.
caveat: The article confirms the Western Lands are adjacent to IAD, not within approach/departure surfaces. The exact boundary relationship between the Western Lands site and IAD's approach/departure surface extents was not independently verified in available public documents, but the site description (between Old Ox Road and the airport's runways) and its prior use for a fourth runway support area indicate it is west of the airfield, not under an approach path.

claim: FAA AC 150/5190-4B (Airport Land Use Compatibility) specifically addresses incompatible land uses within and near runway protection zones, including development that could introduce atmospheric interference, obstruction of maneuvering space, or interference with navigational aids.
source_title: Advisory Circular 150/5190-4B — Airport Land Use Compatibility Planning
supporting_excerpt: AC 150/5190-4B is intended to help airports comply with their grant assurances concerning all compatible land use issues, including obstructions and hazard to airport navigation, airport noise, wildlife and bird hazard attractants, and protection of persons and property on the ground. It is critical to maintain unobstructed space for aircraft to maneuver above ground. Further, limiting atmospheric interference (such as the air turbulence from thermal plumes) near airports is critical to maintaining aircraft control.
data_vintage: current (replaces 4A dated 1987 and 2012 RPZ Interim Guidance)
caveat: The full text of AC 150/5190-4B PDF could not be retrieved (403 Forbidden). Supporting excerpt is partially from the argument memo text (which cites this AC) and partially from secondary summaries of the document's stated purpose. Confirm specific provisions against the published document.

claim: Electronic interference from data center infrastructure (servers, UPS systems, diesel generators, HVAC variable-frequency drives) can affect ILS, VOR, and ATC communications; FAA acknowledges that adverse effects of electronic interference can exist without detection by ground monitors.
source_title: FAA Aeronautical Information Manual — Chapter 1, Section 1: Air Navigation
page_or_section: Chapter 1, Section 1 — navigational aid sensitivity to interference
supporting_excerpt: Although NAVAIDs are monitored by electronic detectors, adverse effects of electronic interference, new obstructions, or changes in terrain near the NAVAID can exist without detection by the ground monitors.
airport_or_entity: All airports with NAVAID-dependent instrument approaches
caveat: The AIM does not specifically identify data centers as an EMI source. EMI risk from data center infrastructure is a recognized engineering concern but would require a site-specific interference study for IAD's ILS and VOR installations on or near RWY 19R/1L.
